column11: Claim text_r Table 2 shows the average situational interest of 80 pre-service teachers according to the connection to the reality of the problems. We observe that, for pre-service teachers, word problems were the most interesting (Mw = 3.28, SDw = 1.22), followed by modelling problems (Mm = 3.11, SDm = 1.25) and, finally, intramathematical problems (Mi = 2.92, SDi = 1.24). Again, we conducted a hypothesis test to analyse whether there were significant differences in interest according to the connection with the reality of the problems. The means of interest did not follow a normal distribution either, so we obtained that there are significant differences between at least two types of problems (𝜒𝜒2(2)=16.54, p < 0.01) by applying Friedman’s test. Nemenyi’s test ensured that there were significant differences in task-specific interest between word and modelling problems (p < 0.05), and between intramathematical and word problems (p < 0.01). There were no significant differences between intramathematical and modelling problems (p = 0.46), indicating that word problems were significantly more interesting for pre-service teachers. column11: The coding of this study was extremely challenging for me and I could not complete it. I feel that the replication study is extremely unclear in describing what effects they are trying to replicate. column11:
This is a replication study on the use of a conjugate preparation
for assessing preference. The original study administered a verbal multiple-stimulus-without-replacement
assessment (VMSWO). The replication study includes, in addition, auditive stimuli and, as stated by the authors, "Deviated from the Davis
et al. procedures, in part, for the purposes of efficiency and practicality". Moreover, the original study performed the assessment five times with the participants but the replication did it just once. The replicators argue "We rationalized this to be an acceptable alteration because supplemental data provided by the Davis et al. study showed HP and LP items identified in the first array of sample stimuli were consistent with HP and LP items identified from seven arrays for 70% of participants in their preliminary study."

column29:
Article. The annotation covers OCs of (in)definite articles (a(n)/the). Given
that the ‘zero article’ was disregarded in previous MOS, it was also disregarded here for comparative purposes. The non-suppliance of an article in an (in)definite OC was tagged as omission. Also, given that both definite and indefinite articles were analysed as a single morpheme in previous MOS, we analysed them similarly, even if we are aware that they are better analysed separately as they do not emerge simultaneously (cf. the discussion in Section 4.4). Selection of one article for the other was tagged as ‘mis-selection’. The forms a/an were understood as spelling variants, so selection of one when the other was expected was not tagged as NTLU. Importantly, determining the OC of the/a(n) is based on information-status distinctions deriving from discourse, i.e., on whether the entity has been previously mentioned in the discourse (i.e., discourse-old, topic) or not (i.e., discourse-new, focus), and therefore whether or not the referent is known to the reader. Articles were annotated independently of the appearance of characters in the picture story, which could give the sense of old information, but technically introduce discoursenew information when retelling the story to a reader. Therefore, ILA considers hearer/reader knowledge (and not speaker knowledge) to determine discourse-old/discourse-new distinctions (cf. Hawkins, 2001).

column25: I do not consider this to be a direct replication study because the authors used a different method to overcome a methodological/conceptual limitation of the original study. Even if the phenomenon being studied is the same, the introduction of a method to measure the duration of events significantly alters the experimental approach. It is not a replication study, but a reformulation of the original study using a different methodological approach. The authors state: "Our primary aim was to address the identified methodological limitation observed in Sastre et al.'s (under review) research, where participants reported the start times for events, and the end time was deduced as the moment they initiated the survey. However, concerns arose about the precision of calculations for daily event durations due to reliance on participants' time inputs. To overcome this limitation, our study conducted a replication of Sastre et al.'s (under review), employing nightly segmentation methods with time-stamped pictures inspired by a previous study".

Fig. 1 shows that our replications produced weaker results
than those reported in the original studies. In our replications,
the effect of God salience on AI reliance is not statistically
different from zero (Studies 1, 2a, 2b, 3, and 5 produced effect
sizes, measured by r, of 0.03, 0.02, 0.03, 0.002, and 0.01,
respectively—in contrast to the original effect sizes reported
for each of the respective studies of 0.19, 0.15, 0.14, 0.11, and
0.19). Fig. 1 omits a conceptual replication of Study 1 that
produced a nonsignificant effect in the opposite direction of
the original Study 1, t(279) = −1.78, P = 0.077, r = −0.10.....Although the majority of our replications produced results directionally
consistent with those of Karataş and Cutright, our results
imply that if the effect exists, it is so small that the original
studies lacked the power to detect it.

Therefore, 120 pp were in the RB task of which 30 were in the RB-S group (one of which was excluded) and 30 were in the RB-R group. This means N = 59 were in the two groups of interest, which also corresponds to the degrees of freedom of 57 in the targeted t-test.

In Problem 2 (N = 155), 22% chose the sure loss (Program C: 400 people die, p < .05), while 78% chose the risky option (Program D: 1/3 probability nobody dies).

The results are consistent with multinational spillovers, though without controls for individual and establishment heterogeneity, the result is difficult to interpret.", "This is the main contribution and new result of this paper. When multinational workers leave multinational establishments and are rehired at domestic establishments, the wages of continuing domestic workers increase. This avenue for multinational spillovers, to my knowledge, has not previously been explored. At the average wage for a typical domestic worker of $3,841 (R$6,522 at average annual exchange rates during the 1996–2001 period), this is an increase of approximately $23 per year per worker, equivalent to one more month of job tenure within the establishment. While this may seem to be a small impact, it is also an appropriately sized impact for the average worker. More important, these estimates are worker-level wage spillovers and not plant-level productivity spillovers, as in previous studies. For the average domestic stablishment in Brazil, with a workforce of approximately sixty, the total implied wage effect from 10 percentage point increase in the share of former multinational workers is roughly $1,400 per year. According to RAIS, in 1998 there were 1,795,798 establishments in Brazil, approximately 98% of which were domestically owned. Therefore, this average impact has the potential to generate $2.5 billion in wage spillovers across all of Brazil (in the range of 0.3% of GDP)."

First, the data support the culpable-control model's assumption that there are two important sources of evaluation in this scenario: the physician's decision to go along with or to violate the hospital's policy, and the patient's death or survival. The results show that the physician in Hitchcock and Knobe's original scenario would have been viewed very negatively if not for the fortuitous outcome of the patient's recovery, and he was not viewed very positively even with this happy consequence. These findings are consistent with the culpable-control assumption that the physician's decision to contravene hospital policy provided a strong initial basis for blame. When the patient died as a result, this negative outcome counted as a severely aggravating circumstance that further elevated the physician's perceived causal role. However, when the physician was viewed positively for following the hospital's policy, he was not viewed as any more causal as a result of the patient's death in comparison to when the patient survived."

Mediation analyses involve the speci- fication of a causal model between three variables and the strengths of the paths between them using multiple regression (see Figure 2). They are designed to determine whether the effect of one variable (in our case, the description of determinism: N&K’s vs. NMNT’s) on another variable (MR⁄FW judgments) is mediated by a third variable (Bypassing). If the description of determinism no longer has a significant effect on MR⁄FW once Bypassing is taken into account, then mediation obtains, which provides evidence that the difference between N&K’s and NMNT’s descriptions of determinism makes a difference to people’s judgments about MR⁄FW because of the difference in the degree to which people interpret the descriptions to involve bypassing.
And this is exactly what we found.

The result we obtained is similar to Nichols’, but different from the result we obtained replicating his study. In any event, the answers to this question were predominantly along the lines of an externalist prediction. The answers to the Believes and Herself Thinks questions, by contrast, tended to fall in line with the internalist prediction (with 95% confidence, the difference in positive answers between Understands and Believes falls within a 15–44% interval, while that between Understands and Herself Thinks falls within a 12–40% interval). This indicates that the choice of question is not innocuous. Moreover, since internalism is standardly understood as a claim about what is required for moral belief or for what agents themselves think is morally right or wrong, rather than for moral understanding, we should primarily focus on the Believes and Herself Thinks questions. The answers to these questions give us no ground for saying that intuitions of defenders of internalism are more theoretically biased than those of externalists, as a majority of subjects were unwilling to attribute moral belief to Anna. Taking the answers of this study at face value, the folk are as divided in their intuitions as are philosophers.10 Moreover, since internalist constraints seem to be widely operative in folk attributions of moral belief, it is at least possible that folk intuitions of moral disagreement are driven by an understanding of the practical role of moral beliefs and moral claims, as noncognitivist internalists would suggest. The study thus leaves us where we started: internalists will have to explain why many are willing to attribute belief in the absence of motivation, just as externalists will have to explain why many are unwilling to do so."

column30: "In column 1, I estimate multinational wage spillovers by pooled ordinary least squares. The results are consistent with multinational spillovers, though without controls for individual and establishment heterogeneity, the result is difficult to interpret.", "This is the main contribution and new result of this paper. When multinational workers leave multinational establishments and are rehired at domestic establishments, the wages of continuing domestic workers increase. This avenue for multinational spillovers, to my knowledge, has not previously been explored. At the average wage for a typical domestic worker of $3,841 (R$6,522 at average annual exchange rates during the 1996–2001 period), this is an increase of approximately $23 per year per worker, equivalent to one more month of job tenure within the establishment. While this may seem to be a small impact, it is also an appropriately sized impact for the average worker. More important, these estimates are worker-level wage spillovers and not plant-level productivity spillovers, as in previous studies. For the average domestic stablishment in Brazil, with a workforce of approximately sixty, the total implied wage effect from 10 percentage point increase in the share of former multinational workers is roughly $1,400 per year. According to RAIS, in 1998 there were 1,795,798 establishments in Brazil, approximately 98% of which were domestically owned. Therefore, this average impact has the potential to generate $2.5 billion in wage spillovers across all of Brazil (in the range of 0.3% of GDP)."

column30: It is clear from the data above that subjects’ evaluations are influenced by the nominal transactions. The modal ranking, chosen by roughly half the subjects, was Carl first, Ben second, and Adam third. Thus, Carl, the only one to make a nominal gain (but a real loss), was the modal choice for the best deal. Adam, who was the only one to make a real gain (but a nominal loss), was the modal choice for the worst deal. Ben, who suffered a 1 percent real and nominal loss, was ranked above Adam, who had a 2 percent real profit but a large nominal loss, and below Carl, who had a 2 percent real loss but a large nominal gain. We have replicated this pattern in another version of this problem involving 2 percent inflation or deflation.

State anxiety was negatively correlated with heart rate during the angry-faces block (r = −.30, p = .049) and not during the neutral-faces block (r = −.16, p = .27) or the happy-faces block (r = −0.12, p = .42). Viewing angry faces significantly slowed participants' heart rates, indicating a freezing response to social threat. No similar effects were found for neutral or happy faces, suggesting the effect is specific to threat-related stimuli.
